gui.distantstock.manual.p1: Place and unlock a Stock Link on the warehouse server; it is published to every connected server. A player on any server opens an untuned terminal, picks a network from the open list, and never has to visit the warehouse. Right-click a transmitter with a joined terminal to copy it in.
gui.distantstock.manual.p2: The warehouse can use the pale-blue Distant Packager. It keeps Create packing logic and produces Distant Parcels. Face the dock cabin toward the operator and leave the sides free for a belt or hopper. An import dock matches address only (blank = *). A parcel in the bay means the slots are occupied.
gui.distantstock.manual.p3: Players never type an IP. OP runs /distantstock, or sneak-clicks a monitor. Pick Host (warehouse) or Client (outer), fill self id, listen, peer, password. Save writes this server's config/distantstock-common.toml and restarts the listener. Same password on every side.
gui.distantstock.manual.p4: One warehouse, many survival servers. Orders carry from=self.id. After packing, the warehouse POSTs the package only to that origin. Outer servers pull /stock from the host only. Outer servers do not act as warehouses for each other.
gui.distantstock.manual.p5: Goggles show live data only: dock mode, short freq or address, UP/DOWN, slots or backlog. Desk: freq, address, catalog size. Monitor: TPS and queue. The tutorial lives in this book. Set giveManual=false to stop handing one out on first join.

block.distantstock.dock.desc: Full casing, pipes into the sides and a fallback face underneath that needs a chute. Lamp: off = offline, green = standby, cyan blinking = dispatching, orange blinking = fallback blocked, red = fault.
block.distantstock.tower_casing.desc: Decorative casing with connected textures on all six faces. A redstone signal turns the centre of linked casings into a see-through window; the propagation range is configurable.
block.distantstock.tower_core.desc: The centre of the tower’s 3x3 base, driven by rotation from below. Stack couplers on top of it and cap them with an ether resonator to raise a tower.
block.distantstock.tower_coupler.desc: A segment of the mast. The taller the stack, the higher the tier — and the more distant devices and chunks it carries.
block.distantstock.ether_resonator.desc: The cap. Turning arms mean the tower is running; it only starts once the tower is complete.
block.distantstock.gauge.desc: A stock desk for the floor. Write to it with a terminal that has joined a network.
block.distantstock.monitor.desc: Wall dashboard: local/peer TPS and link pressure. OP sneak-click opens link setup.
block.distantstock.remote_packager.desc: A pale-blue Create packager variant. It keeps addresses and contents while producing Distant Parcels.

distantstock.ponder.distant_export.text_: Every parcel begins in storage. Set a Distant Packager against the chest and turn it to face the line: when an order arrives it seals the goods into a Distant Parcel and hands it on by itself.
This is the dock, the one door the goods leave through. It holds a single parcel at a time, so everything upstream of it is a queue rather than a buffer.
A belt joins the two. Keep the run flat and let its last block point into the dock: the parcel is handed over as it arrives, with nobody standing there to feed it in.
With a parcel aboard, the lift rises and passes it through the ether surface. The two stock networks stay separate throughout: only the sealed parcel crosses between them.
The underside is the fallback face, and it cannot be seen from here. Leave it clear, or a parcel that comes back will have nowhere to go.
distantstock.ponder.distant_import.text_: On the receiving server the dock needs a delivery address, not a destination. Sneak-click it with a Distant Terminal and the address is written.

A hopper gathers what the dock releases from underneath, and the belt carries it on to storage. The same two blocks serve the other direction as well, which is why the fallback face is worth keeping clear.
The far end is an ordinary chest. Nothing here knows what the goods cost on the other server, and nothing there knows what became of them here; the parcel is the only thing that travelled.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tune.text_1: The Request Desk is the terminal in furniture form. It carries the same network and the same address, so an order written here is an order the packing line can read.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tune.text_2: Sneak-click a dock with a tuned Distant Terminal and it joins the system you have selected; click it plainly and it sends to that system. The desk reports what it did in the line above your hotbar.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tune.text_3: The desk is a place to stand and write, not a machine on the goods path. Give it its own spot beside the line, where the belt will not have to route around it later.
distantstock.ponder.distant_status.text_: The glass lid is the link light. It stays dull while the far side is out of reach, and lights when the two ends find each other, so a glance from across the room is enough to tell whether the line is up.
The wall monitor keeps a longer record: which links are up, how much each side is carrying, and the coordinates of any link that has dropped.
Clearing a fault is deliberate. A dock that has given up waits at red until someone right-clicks it, so a failure cannot be mistaken for an idle machine and quietly forgotten.

The lamp, in order of how much it wants your attention: dark for no network, green for standing by, cyan for a parcel on its way up, orange for cargo waiting on a blocked fallback face, and red for a fault.

Everything the far server will not accept leaves through the underside and waits there. Give it a container or a belt to fall into; with nothing below, the dock holds the cargo and blinks orange until you make room.

distantstock.ponder.distant_tower.text_1: A tower is driven from below: one vertical shaft, set directly under the base. The underside is the only face that takes rotation, so a shaft run in from the side meets nothing. Speed is not the price — a medium network will do; what a tower spends is stress.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tower.text_2: Above the shaft goes the Interlink Tower Base — the one part of a tower that turns, and the one that keeps the count. Close the base off with a 3x3 ring of Distant Casing: the casing has no say in whether a tower stands, but it is the base's face.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tower.text_3: Stack Interlink Tower Couplers upward, and keep the mast unbroken from the base: one gap, or one segment of another block, and there is no tower at all. Five segments is the first tier.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tower.text_4: Cap the mast with an Ether Resonator and the tower is up. The column over the cap is its state lamp: grey while the tower is unfinished or standing still, cyan while it works, and a deeper, self-lit blue while a parcel crosses it.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tower.text_5: Height is rank: five couplers is tier I, two more takes the next step, and seventeen couplers is the last of them, tier VII.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tower.text_6: A tier decides three things: how many distant devices the tower carries (8 at tier I, 128 at VII), how far from the base they may stand (32 blocks out to 144), and how large a square of chunks it keeps loaded (1x1 up to 7x7).
distantstock.ponder.distant_tower.text_7: The shaft below feeds the tower rotation, and taller towers draw more of it: 256 at tier I, roughly doubling a step to 16384 at VII. Fall below a medium speed, or overstress the network, and the light goes out.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tower.text_8: Pull the lever and the casing it lights turns its centre into a see-through window, spreading along the casings it touches. It is decoration only — the tower works exactly the same.

gui.distantstock.manual.p7: A dock group is one system: it decides which docks a parcel comes out of. On the terminal, open the Receiving Group field to see the systems you may use, or type a name nobody has taken to make a new one. Sneak-click a dock to put it in the system you are pointing at; click it to send to that system. A system you make is yours and starts closed — only you may add docks to it, and only you may send into it. The lock beside it in the list opens it to others; click again to take it back. The Distant Monitor on your tower lists every tower in the system and lets you set each one on its own.
gui.distantstock.manual.p8: A Distant Gauge is a factory gauge that orders for itself: each panel is bound to one warehouse on another server, and when the number the panel reads falls short of the target in its value box it orders the difference — one order at a time, a stack at most, settled when the stock reaches the target or written off after two minutes. Bind a panel by right-clicking it with a tuned terminal, sneak-click to unbind; the four panels can be four different warehouses. The Distant Redstone Requester is the same idea on a pulse: one edge, one order carrying all nine of its slots. An unbound one is simply a redstone requester. Both need a tower that carries them: without one they still read, and they do not order.
distantstock.ponder.distant_replenish.te: A Distant Gauge is a factory gauge that orders for itself. Put a panel on the board, set its item and the amount you want to keep, and that panel will watch the number for you.

Right-click that panel with a tuned Distant Terminal to bind it to that terminal's warehouse and receiving group; sneak-click to unbind. Each of the four panels is bound on its own, so one board can draw from four places.

When the amount falls short of the target it orders the difference. One order at a time: the next one waits until the stock arrives or the first is written off, and a single order never asks for more than a stack.
The Distant Redstone Requester is the same idea on a pulse. Give it its nine items and an address in its own screen, bind it the same way, and one rising edge sends one order.

Both order into a receiving group, the same way an order from the desk does, so the goods arrive at a dock on this side. An unbound Requester is just a redstone requester, and an unbound gauge is just a gauge.
Neither one spends anything without a tower carrying it, so build the tower first.

gui.distantstock.manual.p9: Two towers, two dock groups, three steps. One: both sides need a tower that is turning — a tower carrying its devices is the premise of every distant machine, and one that is not turning carries nothing, so its devices stop and say so in red on the goggles. Two: give each dock its system. Sneak-click a dock with a tuned terminal and it joins the system you have selected. Three: give the sending dock its destination. Click it plainly (no sneak) and it sends to the system you have selected, and switches itself to send. Feed parcels in through a side or the back — belts and hoppers both work. They land in a dock of the other system and come out of a side; the underside is the return face for refused and jammed goods, so leave a container under it. A group decides which docks goods come out of and nothing else; it has no relation to tower tier, and the docks of one system may sit under several towers.
